docs.title: pgtern
docs.text:
A PostgreSQL client for Python, with zero runtime dependencies.

pgtern speaks the PostgreSQL wire protocol directly, in pure Python and the standard library only. There are no C extensions and no build step, so pip install pgtern is the whole setup. It offers a DB-API style interface in two forms: blocking, and asyncio.

import pgtern
from pgtern.rows import dict_row

with pgtern.connect("postgresql://app:secret@localhost/app", row_factory=dict_row) as conn:
    with conn.transaction():
        conn.execute("INSERT INTO notes (body) VALUES (%s)", ["hello"])
    print(conn.execute("SELECT id, body FROM notes ORDER BY id").fetchall())

docs.title: Why pgtern
docs.text:
• No dependencies to manage. The package is a small, readable, pure-Python wheel. There is no dependency tree to pin or scan.
  • Installs anywhere Python runs. No compiler and no system libraries are needed.
  • Secure by default. SCRAM-SHA-256 is verified before a login is accepted, and a password is not sent in plaintext unless you choose sslmode=disable.
  • Blocking and async, one API. The same names and behaviour in pgtern and pgtern.aio.
  • Built for modern deployments. Statements use unnamed prepared statements only, so they work with transaction-mode connection poolers.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• Installation: install the package and check the version.
  • Connecting: DSNs, TLS and failover.
  • Queries and transactions: run statements safely.
  • Connection pools: share connections across a service.
  • Security and TLS: what the client verifies and protects.

docs.title: Connecting
docs.text:
pgtern.connect accepts URL and key=value connection strings, the standard PG* environment variables, Unix sockets, and a list of hosts for failover.

conn = pgtern.connect("postgresql://app@db1.internal,db2.internal/app?sslmode=verify-full&sslrootcert=/etc/ssl/ca.pem")

docs.title: TLS modes
docs.text: disable, allow, prefer, require, verify-ca and verify-full, following the PostgreSQL conventions. See Security and TLS for what each one protects.

docs.title: Failover and session targets
docs.text:
Failover moves to the next host after any startup failure, including a timeout during TLS negotiation.

  • target_session_attrs: read-write, read-only, primary, standby or prefer-standby.
  • hostaddr: connect to an address while keeping the host name for certificate checks.
  • connect_timeout: seconds allowed for each host attempt, from opening the socket to the end of startup. The default is 30. 0 means no limit.

docs.title: Passwords
docs.text: Passwords can come from a .pgpass file (PGPASSFILE or ~/.pgpass). A password file that other users can read is ignored.

docs.title: First query
docs.text:
import pgtern
from pgtern.rows import dict_row

with pgtern.connect("postgresql://app:secret@localhost/app", row_factory=dict_row) as conn:
    row = conn.execute("SELECT %s::int AS n", [1]).fetchone()
    print(row["n"])

Choose a row format with a row factory: tuple_row (the default), dict_row or namedtuple_row. Pass one to connect, or to a single cursor.

The asynchronous version uses the same names:

import asyncio
from pgtern import aio

async def main():
    async with await aio.connect("postgresql://app:secret@localhost/app") as conn:
        cur = await conn.execute("SELECT %s::int", [1])
        print(cur.fetchall())

asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install pgtern

pgtern requires Python 3.11 or newer. It has no runtime dependencies.

To work on pgtern itself, see Development.

docs.title: Binary format
docs.text:
Opt in per statement with binary=True:

with pgtern.connect(dsn) as conn:
    value = conn.execute("SELECT %s::timestamptz", [some_datetime], binary=True).fetchone()[0]

Binary transfer covers integers, floats, booleans, text, bytea, uuid, dates, times, intervals, json and jsonb, numeric results, and one-dimensional arrays of these. Other types use text.

docs.title: executemany
docs.text:
executemany sends the whole batch as one pipelined transaction. In autocommit mode, a failing row rolls back the entire batch. Inside a transaction, it aborts that transaction as usual.

with pgtern.connect(dsn, autocommit=True) as conn:
    conn.cursor().executemany("INSERT INTO events (kind, payload) VALUES (%s, %s)", rows)

docs.title: COPY
docs.text:
For the largest loads, use COPY:

with pgtern.connect(dsn) as conn:
    with conn.cursor().copy("COPY events (kind, payload) FROM STDIN") as copy:
        for kind, payload in rows:
            copy.write_row((kind, payload))

Export uses COPY ... TO STDOUT, read with for chunk in copy or copy.rows(). COPY cannot run inside a pipeline or an executemany batch.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Every exception derives from pgtern.Error. Each common SQLSTATE has its own class, such as UniqueViolation or DeadlockDetected, and each belongs to a broader category, such as IntegrityError:

with pgtern.connect(dsn) as conn:
    try:
        conn.execute("INSERT INTO accounts (id) VALUES (%s)", [1])
    except pgtern.IntegrityError:
        conn.rollback()  # a failed transaction must be rolled back before the block ends

docs.title: Query hooks
docs.text:
A hook sees every statement, its row count and the connection target. It never sees bound parameter values:

from contextlib import contextmanager
import time
import pgtern

@contextmanager
def timing(info):
    started = time.perf_counter()
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        print(f"{info.statement!r} took {time.perf_counter() - started:.3f}s ({info.rowcount} rows)")

remove = pgtern.add_query_hook(timing)

A hook that fails on entry or exit is logged and ignored, so it never changes the result of a statement.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
LISTEN only takes effect in autocommit mode, so connect with autocommit=True:

with pgtern.connect(dsn, autocommit=True) as conn:
    conn.execute("LISTEN orders")
    for note in conn.notifies(timeout=30):
        print(note.channel, note.payload)

The async connection provides the same notifications through async for.

LISTEN needs a session that stays on one server connection, so use a direct connection or session-mode pooling for it.

docs.title: Pipelines
docs.text:
Pipeline mode sends many statements before reading any reply:

with pgtern.connect(dsn) as conn:
    with conn.pipeline() as pipe:
        a = pipe.execute("INSERT INTO queue (job) VALUES (%s)", ["a"])
        b = pipe.execute("SELECT count(*) FROM queue")
    print(b.fetchone())    # results are ready once the block ends

Replies are read in order at each sync point: pipe.sync(), the end of the block, or every batch_size statements. A sync point raises the first failure in its batch, so a failed statement cannot pass silently.

Under autocommit, a sync point is also a commit point, so the statements in one batch succeed or fail together. If the block exits with an exception under autocommit, the batch is rolled back.

Statements after a failure raise pgtern.errors.PipelineAborted. Pipelines support text format only, and COPY cannot run inside one.

docs.title: Connection pools
docs.text:
from pgtern.pool import ConnectionPool

pool = ConnectionPool(dsn, min_size=4, max_size=20, timeout=5)
with pool.connection() as conn:
    conn.execute("SELECT 1")

A pool keeps min_size connections open and grows up to max_size on demand.

The async pool keeps min_size connections open with a background task. It retires connections that have been idle longer than max_idle while the pool is above min_size.

A connection is checked for liveness when it is handed out. It is rolled back if it was returned in the middle of a transaction, and replaced if the server has closed it. A caller that waits longer than timeout seconds receives pgtern.PoolTimeout.

docs.title: Queries and transactions
docs.text:
with pgtern.connect(dsn) as conn:
    conn.execute("CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS accounts (id int PRIMARY KEY, balance numeric)")

    with conn.transaction():               # commits on success, rolls back on error
        conn.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - %s WHERE id = %s", [10, 1])
        conn.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + %s WHERE id = %s", [10, 2])

    cur = conn.execute("SELECT id, balance FROM accounts WHERE balance > %s", [0])
    for row in cur:
        print(row)

Placeholders are %s. Values are sent as parameters and are never interpolated into the SQL text.

docs.title: Building SQL safely
docs.text:
Use the sql module to compose identifiers and literals:

from pgtern import sql

with pgtern.connect(dsn) as conn:
    query = sql.SQL("SELECT * FROM {} WHERE id = %s").format(sql.Identifier("accounts"))
    conn.execute(query, [1])

docs.title: Streaming large results
docs.text:
A named cursor runs on the server and fetches rows in batches, so a result never has to fit in memory:

with pgtern.connect(dsn) as conn:
    with conn.transaction():
        with conn.cursor("big_report") as cur:
            cur.execute("SELECT * FROM events")
            cur.itersize = 1000
            for row in cur:
                process(row)

Server-side cursors support scrollable, withhold and scroll().

docs.title: Values and types
docs.text:
• Python int parameters are sent as int4, int8 or numeric, depending on size. Use an explicit cast such as %s::smallint when a function takes smallint.
  • timestamptz values are returned in UTC, in both text and binary format, with the same tzinfo.
  • Intervals with months or years decode to pgtern.Interval(months, delta), because a month has no fixed length. Other intervals decode to timedelta.
  • A time value of 24:00:00 raises DataError, because Python has no such time.
  • Dates and times follow the session's DateStyle, and text follows its client_encoding. Both are read from the server after every change. Non-ASCII text under a non-UTF-8 encoding raises NotSupportedError before anything is sent.

docs.title: Custom loaders and dumpers
docs.text:
Register loaders for PostgreSQL types and dumpers for Python classes:

from enum import Enum
from pgtern import adapters

class Mood(Enum):
    SAD = "sad"
    HAPPY = "happy"

adapters.register_loader("mood", adapters.enum_loader(Mood))           # CREATE TYPE mood AS ENUM (...)
adapters.register_loader("span", adapters.range_loader(int))           # CREATE TYPE span AS RANGE (subtype = int4)
adapters.register_dumper(Mood, lambda m: m.value)

Loaders are looked up by type name once per connection and cached. A registered loader applies to connections opened afterwards, and to pooled connections when they are next returned to the pool.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
• PostgreSQL: 14, 15, 16, 17 and 18.
  • Python: 3.11, 3.12 and 3.13, tested in continuous integration.
  • Platforms: tested on Linux. Unix sockets, fork() and .pgpass permission checks behave differently on Windows, so check those yourself there.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
Contributions are welcome. pgtern is a small library with a strict scope: zero runtime dependencies, standard library only, and a stable public API.

The full workflow is in CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
pip install -e ".[dev]"
eval "$(scripts/start-test-postgres.sh)"    # throwaway server with SCRAM, MD5, cleartext, trust and TLS users
pytest
scripts/start-test-postgres.sh stop

The unit tests run without a server. The integration tests need PGTERN_TEST_DSN. Optional suites read PGTERN_TEST_POOLER_DSN, which points at a transaction-mode connection pooler, and PGTERN_TEST_RESTART_CMD, a command that restarts the test server.

docs.title: Security policy
docs.text:
Security fixes are released for the most recent minor version of pgtern.

Version Supported 0.4.x Yes < 0.4 No

Report suspected vulnerabilities privately, using GitHub's Security → Report a vulnerability feature on the repository. Do not open a public issue or pull request for a vulnerability.

The full policy is in SECURITY.md.

docs.title: Forking
docs.text:
Do not use a connection across fork(). A forked child that uses an inherited connection gets OperationalError.

A pool resets itself in the child. On first use it discards the parent's connections without closing them, which would otherwise end the parent's sessions, and then opens its own.

docs.title: Limits and safety
docs.text:
• max_result_bytes is a connection attribute that caps the bytes one statement may return. It is None (no cap) by default. A result over the cap is read and discarded, the connection stays usable, and the statement raises DataError. Results are held in memory, so use a server-side cursor for large ones.
  • Reentrancy. Using a connection from inside a COPY block, or from inside a notice or notify handler, raises ProgrammingError at once.
  • Hooks and handlers. A query hook that fails is logged and ignored. A notice or notify handler that raises is logged too.

docs.title: Security and TLS
docs.text:
• Password checks. The server must prove it knows the password before a SCRAM login is accepted.
  • No plaintext passwords by accident. A password is not sent in plaintext unless you choose sslmode=disable. A server that declines TLS under prefer cannot collect it.
  • Certificate verification. verify-ca and verify-full require a root certificate (sslrootcert). They fail rather than fall back to the system store.
  • Channel binding. Over TLS, the login is bound to that connection with SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS (tls-server-end-point, RFC 5929), so a login relayed through another connection fails.
  • Stricter login. Set require_auth=scram-sha-256 to refuse any server that does not use SCRAM, including servers that allow trust authentication.

Under allow and prefer, the client refuses MD5 and cleartext passwords on an unencrypted connection. Under disable it sends them, because encryption was explicitly turned off.

Report vulnerabilities privately, as described in the security policy.
